title: Shloka 103
subtitle: Red, fixed in the flesh, and pleased by jaggery-rice

namas.translation: The colour of Lākinī is plain red, unmixed with any other shade.
Among the bodily constituents she is fixed in the flesh.

compound.gloss: she who is grounded in the flesh

children.gloss: standing firm in, being fixed upon

namas.translation: The offering set before her at this station is rice sweetened with raw cane sugar, and her mind receives it with pleasure.

compound.gloss: she whose mind is pleased by rice cooked with jaggery

namas.gloss: Giver Of Joy To Every Devotee
namas.translation: No worshipper is left out of her generosity; happiness reaches each of them without exception.

compound.gloss: she who gives happiness to all her devotees

namas.translation: Presiding over the maṇipūra station, she takes on the shape of the Tantric goddess Lākinī, addressed with the respectful title of mother.

morphology.note: The having lies in the suffix -in, so lākinyambāsvarūpa is the compound and svarūpiṇī the taddhita made on it; the name is also read as a bahuvrīhi, she who has Mother Lākinī for her form. At this wheel the hymn's pairing of yoginī and cakra agrees with that of the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, though the two schemes part company at other stations.

compound.gloss: she who bears the very form of the mother Lākinī

children.gloss: mother, a title of respect for a woman

commentary.meaning: Five names finish a portrait the previous verse began. There the hymn seated her in the lotus of the navel, gave her three faces, armed her, and surrounded her with attendant goddesses; here it supplies her colour, the layer of the body she governs, the food set before her, the gift she makes, and finally her name. The order is that of an iconographic manual read from the outside inward: what you see, where she lives, what she is given, what she gives, who she is. Only in the last word does the description resolve into a person, and the person is addressed as mother. The fourth name is the one that breaks the pattern. Everything around it is technical — a pigment, a tissue, a dish — and samastabhaktasukhadā is a promise, an unrestricted one. It is worth noticing that the promise is attached not to Lalitā in her sovereign form but to a three-faced yoginī sitting in a wheel of the body, and that the verse ends by insisting the two are not different.
commentary.history:
From the four hundred and seventy-fifth name onward the hymn does something it does nowhere else: it stops praising and starts cataloguing. Seven yoginīs are described in turn, one for each wheel of the yogic body, and each receives the same set of particulars in nearly the same order — the lotus she occupies, the number of her faces, her weapons, her retinue, her colour, the bodily tissue she is lodged in, the cooked food offered to her, sometimes a boon, and last her name. This verse supplies the final five items for the third of the seven. The verse before it has already placed her in the maṇipūra lotus at the navel, given her three faces, put the thunderbolt and other weapons in her hands, and set Ḍāmarī and the rest around her; what remains is colour, flesh, food, gift, and name.

The seven are Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, Hākinī and Yākinī, and even a reader with no Sanskrit can see that they are a series rather than seven independently invented goddesses: one shape, seven initial consonants. The tradition holds the sequence of names fixed but not the wheels they are mapped onto. This hymn runs downward — the throat first, then the heart, then the navel, then the genitals, then the base of the spine — while the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, the late Bengali handbook on which most modern accounts of the cakras ultimately depend, runs upward from the base, and so lands each goddess on a different wheel. The two schemes coincide at the navel, and again at the brow and the crown where the sequences converge; through the lower five they are mirror images. Anyone reading around in the literature will meet both, and the disagreement is about the map, not about the order of the names.

niṣṭhā in māṃsaniṣṭhā is an ordinary noun from ni-√sthā, to stand down or stand firm: a standing-place, a foundation, and in philosophical prose the state in which something finally comes to rest. To call her established in flesh is to say that among the constituents of the body, flesh is where she is grounded. The medical tradition counts seven such constituents: the nutrient fluid, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and the generative essence, each refined out of the one before it. The hymn assigns one to each yoginī, and as the wheels descend the tissues advance along that list — skin for the first, where the physicians would have put rasa; blood for the second; flesh here for the third; fat for the fourth. Read whole, the section claims that the body is not merely where the goddess is worshipped but the material she is distributed through, layer by layer.

Red belongs to the navel by more than convention. Maṇipūra, a word that means something like the city filled with jewels, is where yogic physiology locates the body's fire — the heat that cooks food, and by extension the heat of transformation and appetite. The Bhagavad Gītā's line about the lord becoming the digestive fire in the bodies of living creatures is the classical statement of the idea, and it stands behind this whole cluster: a red goddess, seated at the fire, fixed in flesh, gladdened by a sweet.

Guḍa is cane juice boiled down and left unrefined — jaggery — and guḍānna is rice cooked with it, still made in South Indian kitchens and still offered in temples. Each of the seven receives a different rice: milk-sweetened for the first, rice with ghee for the second, this jaggery rice for the third, curd rice for the fourth, and so on down to the last, who is offered food of every kind. Nothing in the list is exotic. These are the dishes of an ordinary household, and the hymn's claim is that the powers holding the body together are fed by them. Prītamānasā, her mind gladdened, keeps the transaction personal: the offering is not consumed, it is enjoyed.

The boon is where the template loosens. Rākiṇī at the heart is called the giver of boons to great heroes, a phrase with a restriction built into it; Lākinī's title carries none. Samasta means combined, entire, all without remainder, and sukha is not liberation but ease, comfort, ordinary well-being — the flat opposite of duḥkha. Set where it is, between a dish of sweetened rice and the goddess's own name, it reads less as a soteriological promise than as a domestic one, which may be the point. The closing name then makes the identification explicit. Svarūpiṇī means bearing the very form, and whatever has been said of the goddess at the navel is thereby said of the one goddess the hymn has been naming for a thousand names.
commentary.practice:
The verse divides with unusual tidiness. Its four quarters of eight syllables are filled by whole names: two four-syllable names in the first quarter, then a single eight-syllable name in each of the remaining three. Nothing straddles a boundary. Once the first line is secure the rest can be taken a quarter at a time, and a reciter who loses the thread can pick it up at any quarter without reconstructing a compound from the middle.

Māṃsaniṣṭhā is the hard word. It opens with a long ā carrying anusvāra, and the anusvāra here assimilates to the sibilant that follows — a nasalised vowel running into the s, not an English m followed by an s. It closes with ṣṭh, a retroflex sibilant and then an aspirated retroflex stop: the tongue curls back for ṣ and stays back for ṭh, with the breath released after the stop rather than before it. Anyone who produces something like sh-th here has made two dental sounds where the Sanskrit wants two retroflex ones. The same cluster returns two verses later in medoniṣṭhā, so the drill pays twice.

In raktavarṇā, the r of rṇā is a single brief tap made behind the ridge, not the sustained American r, and the ṇ that follows it is retroflex because of it. Guḍānnaprītamānasā looks shapeless and is not: guḍa ends in a short a, anna begins with a short a, and two short a's fuse into one long ā, so the elements are guḍa, anna, prīta and mānasa. Knowing that, you will place the long vowel correctly every time. The doubled nn that follows has to be held — a genuinely long consonant, like the two n's held across the word boundary in English thin nail.

For the recitation performed as archanā, with an offering made at each name, the nominatives become datives. Four of the five here are feminine ā-stems and take -āyai: raktavarṇāyai namaḥ, māṃsaniṣṭhāyai namaḥ, guḍānnaprītamānasāyai namaḥ, samastabhaktasukhadāyai namaḥ. The fifth is not. Svarūpiṇī is an ī-stem, and its dative is -ṇyai — lākinyambāsvarūpiṇyai namaḥ. The closing names of the other yoginīs, which end in the same way, behave the same way, so this is worth fixing once rather than being caught by it repeatedly.

As for what the verse asks: it is the third instalment of a survey that refuses to leave the body out of the worship. A chanter who has spent the preceding stretch of the hymn on cosmology and titles of sovereignty now finds the goddess located in his own flesh, fed with a sweet made of boiled cane juice, and called mother. The traditional use of this section is in nyāsa, where the practitioner touches the successive stations of the body while naming who occupies them; done that way the verse is not a description of anatomy but an address to it. Even chanted straight through it pulls the attention downward, from the hymn's abstractions to the navel, where digestion is going on while one recites.

crossReferences.iast: ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ deham āśritaḥ | prāṇāpānasamāyuktaḥ pacāmy annaṃ caturvidham ||
crossReferences.translation: Becoming the fire that belongs to all men, I take up residence in the bodies of living creatures; joined with the in-breath and the out-breath, I cook the four kinds of food.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest and clearest version of what this verse assumes without arguing for it. The digestive fire at the navel is not a metaphor for the divine presence but an instance of it, and the deity is on both sides of the meal at once — the one who eats the offering and the heat that digests it. Read alongside guḍānnaprītamānasā it explains why a goddess seated at the maṇipūra should be characterised by a dish of rice.

crossReferences.iast: annaṃ brahmeti vyajānāt | annād dhy eva khalv imāni bhūtāni jāyante | annena jātāni jīvanti | annaṃ prayanty abhisaṃviśanti ||
crossReferences.translation: He came to know that food is brahman. For it is indeed from food that these beings are born; being born they live by food; and into food they pass and are absorbed when they depart.
crossReferences.relevance: Bhṛgu's first answer, the one he is sent back to improve on. It is the conviction that keeps the food-offerings in this section from being decoration: anna is where the enquiry into the absolute begins, and the section of the hymn that names the tissues of the body also names what feeds them. The Upaniṣad goes on past food to breath, mind and bliss; the hymn, characteristically, keeps all of them.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library; frequently reprinted)
references.note: The only full English access to the commentary that most reciters have heard of. Through the yoginī section it is largely occupied with matching each name against a fixed list of particulars, which is exactly what a reader needs here — it shows that the section is a system rather than a heap of epithets. The English is stiff and the transliteration old-fashioned; use it for the structure, not the prose.

references.title: The Serpent Power: The Secret of Tantra Yoga
references.author: Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe) (1919; Dover and Ganesh reprints)
references.note: Still the usual English route to the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, which is the text behind the rival assignment of the seven yoginīs to the wheels. Skip the long introduction, which is Edwardian in its physiology and its confidence, and read the translated verses with their commentary. Doing so is the fastest way to see that the scheme in this hymn is one option among several rather than the received map.

references.title: The Roots of Ayurveda: Selections from Sanskrit Medical Writings
references.author: tr. Dominik Wujastyk (Penguin Classics, 3rd ed. 2003)
references.note: Read the selections from the Caraka and Suśruta compendia to find out what a dhātu is before deciding what māṃsaniṣṭhā means. The medical texts treat flesh as one stage in a chain of refinements from food to semen, and once that chain is in view the hymn's distribution of seven tissues across seven goddesses stops looking arbitrary.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: The best scholarly account of the tradition that transmits this hymn, and useful here specifically for its treatment of how a South Indian brahmin lineage absorbed a body of practice full of yoginīs, flesh and food offerings. It explains the social setting in which a verse like this one is chanted daily and unremarkably.
